short: This entry collects the forkhead factors whose preferred site is not the ordinary RYAAAYA element. Two things are going on. FOXN1 and FOXN4 read a completely unrelated five-base sequence, GACGC, called the forkhead-like or FHL motif, using the same recognition helix in a shifted register; FOXN2, FOXN3, FOXJ2 and FOXJ3 are bispecific and bind both FHL and canonical sites. Separately, the FOXP proteins (FOXP1-4) are the only forkheads that can form a domain-swapped dimer, and their highest-information models are a head-to-head pair of forkhead half-sites rather than a single one. The factors matter clinically: FOXN1 loss causes human athymic immunodeficiency, FOXP2 a speech disorder, and FOXP3 the autoimmune syndrome IPEX.
long:
## The factors

Seven of the human forkhead proteins sit here. FOXN1 is restricted to thymic epithelium and skin
keratinocytes; FOXN4 to retinal and spinal neural progenitors; FOXN2, FOXN3, FOXJ2 and FOXJ3 are
broadly expressed. FOXP1, FOXP2 and FOXP4 are expressed in brain, lung, heart and lymphocytes,
and FOXP3 almost only in regulatory T cells. All carry the same ~100-residue winged-helix domain
as the rest of the family - three alpha-helices on a small beta-sheet, with wing 1 and wing 2
gripping the backbone - so nothing about the fold predicts their unusual specificity. What
distinguishes the FOXP subfamily structurally is a single substitution: a proline conserved in
other FOX proteins is an alanine in FOXP1-4, which allows the domain to swap helices with a
second copy of itself. In the FOXP2 and FOXP3 crystal structures the swapped dimer is real, and
in the FOXP3 ternary complex with NFAT1 on the interleukin-2 promoter it bridges two separate
DNA duplexes rather than two half-sites on one. IPEX-causing FOXP3 mutations map either to the
DNA-binding surface or to this dimer interface, and interface mutants bind DNA normally but
cannot suppress T cell activation.

## The motif

There is no single consensus for this family, which is why one is not given. The FHL site is
GACGC, five bases with no resemblance to RYAAAYA. The FOXN1 co-crystal structure at 1.6 A shows
why the same protein can read either: the recognition helix sits in the major groove in both
cases, but the FKH and FHL sequences are contacted in two distinct modes with partially
different registers, using a mixture of direct and water-mediated hydrogen bonds, and a single
alternative side-chain rotamer in the recognition helix is a major determinant of which mode is
used. The FoxN3 structures make the same point from the other side: FoxN3 adopts essentially one
conformation on both sites and uses the same amino acids to touch different bases, while the DNA
shape differs between the two complexes. Bispecificity of this kind has arisen repeatedly and
independently in forkhead evolution and is generally not explained by changes in the known
specificity-determining residues. The FOXP side of the family looks different again. Most FOXP
models here are ordinary canonical sites (JASPAR FOXP1, FOXP2, FOXP3, FOXP4 all GTAAACA;
HOCOMOCO FOXP1 TGTTTACT), but the highest-information models, CIS-BP FOXP3 (25.6 bits) and
Vierstra AC0285 (24.8 bits), are ATTTGTCATACAAAT: two RYAAAYA half-sites in their ACAAAT flavor,
facing each other, with a three-base spacer. Whether that arrangement is bound by the domain-
swapped dimer or by two independent monomers is not settled by the available structures, which
show the swapped dimer holding two different DNA molecules.

## Where it acts

Because GACGC is only five bases, it is expected several million times in the genome and carries
almost no positional information on its own; FOXN1 needs its C-terminal region for high-affinity
binding, and its affinity drops on DNA containing 5-methylcytosine, so methylation state and
flanking sequence matter more here than for canonical forkhead sites. FOXN1 acts at thymic
epithelial enhancers controlling the genes that make the thymus permissive for T cell
development, and at hair keratin genes in skin. FOXP1 and FOXP2 occupy large numbers of distal
sites in brain and lymphoid cells, often with co-repressors of the NuRD and CtBP families rather
than with a named composite element; FOXP3 works in a multiprotein complex on T cell enhancers
together with NFAT, RUNX1 and ETS factors, which is how the IL2 promoter site was solved. JASPAR
contains a CAP-SELEX composite, FOXJ2::ELF1, in which most of the information is the ETS GGAA
core.

## Biology and disease

FOXN1 null mice and rats are the classical nude strains: no thymus, no hair. Human FOXN1
mutations produce the same picture - congenital alopecia, nail dystrophy and severe T cell
deficiency - and the human nude phenotype was the first clinical description of this. FOXP2 was
identified through a family with a severe developmental speech and language disorder segregating
with a forkhead-domain mutation. FOXP3 mutations cause IPEX (immune dysregulation,
polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked), and FOXP3 is the lineage-defining factor of
regulatory T cells. FOXP1 haploinsufficiency causes intellectual disability with autistic
features, and FOXP1 is recurrently translocated and overexpressed in diffuse large B-cell
lymphoma and MALT lymphoma. FOXN3 and FOXJ3 have weaker phenotypes; FOXN4 is required for
retinal amacrine and horizontal cell production.

## Reading a hit

A GACGC match alone means very little: five bases, no degeneracy assumed, and no way to tell
FOXN1 from FOXN4 or from a bispecific FOXN2/FOXN3 or FOXJ2/FOXJ3. Use it only in combination
with expression evidence or with a longer model that includes the flanks. A canonical RYAAAYA
match cannot be assigned to this family at all, since FOXP1-4, FOXJ2, FOXJ3, FOXN2 and FOXN3 all
also read the ordinary site and are indistinguishable there from the 40-odd other forkheads. The
dimeric ATTTGTCATACAAAT model is specific enough to be worth something, but it appears in only
two of the 29 models here and is labelled FOXP3 in one database and simply "FOXP" in the other.
HOCOMOCO contains no FOXN model at all; the two CIS-BP FOXN entries (FOXN1, 3.3 bits; FOXN4, 5.2
bits) are inferred from mouse proteins at 99% and 95% DNA-binding-domain identity. Treat
FOXJ2::ELF1 as an ETS motif: its nearest neighbors across all four databases are ETV-family
motifs, not forkhead ones.
caveats: Moderate confidence in the family as a concept, low confidence in member assignment. The FHL site GACGC is too short to be informative alone and is not distinguishable between FOXN1, FOXN4 and the bispecific FOXN2/FOXN3, FOXJ2/FOXJ3 proteins. Most FOXP and FOXJ models in these databases are ordinary RYAAAYA sites, so a hit on them says "forkhead", not "divergent forkhead". Only two models capture the FOXP head-to-head arrangement. The FOXN1 and FOXN4 CIS-BP models are inferred from mouse orthologs, and HOCOMOCO has no FOXN entry. The JASPAR FOXJ2::ELF1 composite is dominated by its ETS half and its nearest neighbors are ETS motifs.
